Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

# Why we're hiring for developer relations

We shipped an API two years ago and mostly stopped talking about it. Adoption grew anyway, which was flattering and also a problem: we had no idea what people were doing with it. Support tickets were our only signal, and support tickets skew toward the moment something breaks.

So we're building a developer relations team. Three people to start, reporting into product rather than marketing. That reporting line is deliberate. We don't want a team whose job is to generate impressions.

The first thing they'll do is unglamorous. Our quickstart takes 40 minutes to get to a first successful call, and about a third of people abandon partway through. We know this from instrumentation, not intuition. Fixing that is worth more than any conference talk we could give this year.

After that, the work is mostly listening. Sitting in on integration calls. Reading the Discord instead of skimming it. Writing down the questions that come up repeatedly and turning them into either docs or, more often, API changes. Our webhook retry semantics confuse nearly everyone who touches them; that's a design problem wearing a documentation costume.

There's a business case, and it's ordinary. Developers evaluate tools before anyone signs a contract. If evaluation is painful, we lose deals we never hear about. Fixing that is cheaper than sales.

We're hiring two developer advocates and a docs engineer. Postings go up next week.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- paragraph_uniformity (5 paragraphs, spread 0.24):

Return only the rewritten text.

We shipped an API two years ago and mostly stopped talking about it. Adoption grew anyway, which was flattering and also a problem: we had no idea what people were doing with it. Support tickets were our only signal, and support tickets skew toward the moment something breaks. That gave us a picture of our product assembled entirely from its failures, which is a strange way to run a company.

So we're building a developer relations team. Three people to start, reporting into product rather than marketing. That reporting line is deliberate. We don't want a team whose job is to generate impressions.

The first thing they'll do is unglamorous. Our quickstart takes 40 minutes to get to a first successful call, and about a third of people abandon partway through. We know this from instrumentation, not intuition. Fixing that is worth more than any conference talk we could give this year.

After that, the work is mostly listening: sitting in on integration calls, reading the Discord instead of skimming it, writing down the questions that come up over and over and turning them into either docs or, more often, API changes. Our webhook retry semantics confuse nearly everyone who touches them, and no amount of prose will fix a design problem. There's a business case too, and it's ordinary. Developers evaluate tools before anyone signs a contract. If evaluation is painful, we lose deals we never hear about, and fixing that is cheaper than sales.

We're hiring two developer advocates and a docs engineer. Postings go up next week.
